description: Plot vs story, three-act structure, Todorov's equilibrium, and how narrative shapes meaning.
content_html:
Plot and Story Are Not the Same Thing

When people say “what’s the film about?” they are really asking two separate questions at once. The first is about the plot — the order in which the film chooses to show us events. The second is about the story — the full, chronological sequence of everything that happens in the film’s world, including events we never see. Russian literary theorists called these two concepts syuzhet (plot — the arrangement on screen) and fabula (story — the underlying chronology). Understanding the gap between them is essential for film analysis, because a director’s choice about what to show, when to show it, and what to withhold is a primary tool for creating meaning and shaping spectator response.

Key Fact

Plot (syuzhet) is the arrangement of events on screen — the order a director chooses. Story (fabula) is the full chronology of events in the film’s world. A film that opens with its ending and then flashes back has the same story as one that tells events in order, but a radically different plot.

Three-Act Structure

The most widely used narrative framework in mainstream cinema is the three-act structure. Act 1 establishes the world of the film, introduces the main character and their ordinary situation, and ends with an inciting incident that forces the protagonist into a new situation. Act 2 is the longest section — typically around half the film — in which the protagonist pursues a goal against escalating obstacles, building to a crisis point or plot point that forces a decisive choice. Act 3 drives toward the climax and then delivers a resolution that answers the central dramatic question.

It is important to understand that three-act structure is a useful analytical framework, not a rigid prescription. Many films — particularly independent and global cinema — subvert or abandon it deliberately. When they do, the departure itself becomes meaningful: a film that refuses a clear resolution leaves the spectator in productive discomfort, and that discomfort is part of what the director is communicating.

Cause and Effect, Ellipsis and Withholding

Mainstream narrative is driven by cause and effect: every scene is motivated by something that came before it, and produces consequences that drive the next. This logic keeps audiences engaged because they are constantly asking “what happens next?” and “why did that happen?” When cause and effect is disrupted — when a film jumps to a new scene without explaining the connection — the spectator becomes aware of the narration itself, which can feel disorienting or thought-provoking depending on the filmmaker’s intent.

Ellipsis is the standard tool for compressing story time. A cut from one scene to a scene set weeks later is an ellipsis: the film has omitted the intervening time. Almost every narrative film uses ellipsis constantly. The meaningful question is what the film chooses to leave out — ellipsis is a selective act. Withholding information is a more active version of the same technique: the director deliberately keeps something from the audience to create suspense, mystery, or a later revelation. A thriller may conceal the identity of a killer; a drama may conceal a character’s true motive; a non-linear film may omit a scene that would explain everything until the very end. In each case, what the spectator does not know shapes how they experience the whole film.

Tzvetan Todorov, a Bulgarian literary theorist, proposed that most stories follow a three-stage pattern: equilibrium (an initial state of normality or balance), disruption (an event that breaks that balance and creates conflict), and new equilibrium (a restored state of normality, which may differ from the original). This framework is genuinely useful for identifying what changes across a narrative and how the film positions change as desirable, inevitable, or ambiguous.

However, a very common exam error is to describe Todorov’s model in the abstract — listing the three stages without applying them to a specific moment in the film. The way to use this theory effectively is to identify the moment of disruption by name and explain what specific filmic choices the director uses to signal that the equilibrium has broken. For instance: in a film where the protagonist’s ordinary world is established through a quiet domestic scene, the disruption might be marked by a sudden change in lighting state, an abrupt edit, or the introduction of a character-associated leitmotif. Pinning the theory to a named moment with specific micro-features earns marks; describing the theory in the abstract does not.

Key Fact

Todorov’s model (equilibrium → disruption → new equilibrium) is a tool for analysis, not a plot summary template. Use it to identify what changes in a film and then explain which specific shots, edits, or sound choices signal that change to the spectator.

Non-Linear Narrative and Spectator Positioning

When a film tells its story out of chronological order, it is making an active choice about what the spectator will know, and when. A film that opens with a death and then flashes back to show us how it happened positions us with superior knowledge — we watch every scene asking “does this lead to what we already know?” This technique, known as dramatic irony at a narrative level, changes the kind of suspense the film creates: instead of “what will happen?” we ask “how did it happen?” and “could it have been otherwise?” David Bordwell, the film theorist, argues that narration is essentially the formal organisation of story information. Every narrative choice — the order of scenes, the use of ellipsis, the timing of revelations — is a decision about what the spectator needs to feel and understand at each moment.

For global English-language cinema in particular, narrative innovation often carries thematic weight. A fractured, non-linear structure in a film about memory signals that memory itself is unreliable; a film about trauma that refuses a clean new equilibrium signals that some disruptions do not resolve. When you analyse narrative in the exam, ask not just what the structure is, but why that structure is the right one for that film’s subject matter.

Vladimir Propp studied Russian folk tales and identified recurring character roles he called character functions: the hero (who seeks a goal), the villain (who opposes the hero), the donor (who provides a magical gift or piece of knowledge), the helper (who assists the hero), the dispatcher (who sends the hero on the quest), the princess (the goal or reward), and the false hero (who initially appears heroic but is not). These functions are most clearly visible in mainstream genre films such as action, adventure or horror. Like Todorov, Propp is useful at GCSE level when applied to a named moment rather than mapped wholesale onto an entire film. Asking “who performs the donor function in this film, and in which scene?” is a sharper analytical question than “this film follows Propp’s model.”
exam_tip_html: For questions on narrative, the most common error is confusing analysis with plot summary. If your answer describes what happens in chronological order, you are summarising the story, not analysing the plot. To shift into analysis, ask yourself: “why does the director choose to show this event at this moment, in this way?” For an 8-mark analysis of narrative structure, anchor Todorov’s model or the three-act framework to a specific named scene — identify the inciting incident by name, state what filmic choices (a change in lighting, an edit, a sound design shift) signal the disruption to the spectator, and explain what that does to the audience’s experience. For a 5-mark explain-effect question on narrative, the mark scheme rewards identifying a technique (e.g. ellipsis, withholding information, non-linear structure), naming a moment where it appears, and stating the effect on the spectator. One sentence per mark is a reliable discipline: claim, evidence, effect.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Plot (syuzhet) is the order of events as shown on screen; story (fabula) is the full chronological sequence — the gap between them is where a director makes meaning.
  • Three-act structure (set-up, confrontation, resolution) is the dominant framework in mainstream cinema; non-linear narratives that subvert it do so for thematic reasons the analysis must explain.
  • Todorov’s model (equilibrium, disruption, new equilibrium) is only valuable when applied to a named moment with specific micro-features — describing it in the abstract earns no marks.

practice_questions.text: What term describes the full chronological sequence of events in a film's world, including events not shown on screen?
What is meant by 'ellipsis' as a narrative technique in film?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that ellipsis compresses time by omitting events; 1 mark for explaining the effect: it jumps forward in time without showing the intervening period, allowing the film to focus on what matters and withhold what it chooses.

practice_questions.text: Choose a film you have studied and identify its inciting incident by name. Explain how one specific filmic choice signals this disruption to the spectator.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for naming the film; 1 mark for identifying the inciting incident by name or descriptive label; 1 mark for identifying a specific filmic choice at that moment (e.g. a change in lighting, an abrupt edit, a shift in score); 1 mark for explaining how that choice signals disruption to the spectator; 1 mark for accurate use of specialist vocabulary (e.g. inciting incident, disruption, non-diegetic, continuity editing).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how narrative structure in a named sequence from a film you have studied shapes the spectator's experience. In your answer, apply either Todorov's equilibrium model or the three-act framework to a specific named moment, linking at least two micro-level filmic choices to the structural function of that moment.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The answer names the film and a specific sequence; applies Todorov or three-act structure to that named moment with precision (e.g. identifies the moment of disruption and the filmic choices that signal it); at least two micro-level choices (editing, sound, cinematography) are linked to the structural function of the moment; the analysis explains what the structural choice does for the spectator, not just what happens; specialist vocabulary is used precisely (equilibrium, disruption, inciting incident, plot point, cause and effect, ellipsis).
Secure: Named film and sequence; theory applied to a moment; at least one micro-level choice linked to structural function; effect on spectator present; specialist vocabulary mostly accurate.
Developing: Theory described in the abstract without being applied to a named moment; or moment identified but micro-level choices absent; effect on spectator implied rather than stated.
Emerging: Plot summary with a theory name dropped in; no named moment; no micro-level analysis; descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how one specific narrative technique (such as non-linear structure, withholding information, or ellipsis) is used in a short sequence from a film you have studied to position the spectator. Name the film and the sequence. Refer to at least three distinct features of the sequence in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Stays tightly within one named sequence; narrative technique is identified precisely and applied to that sequence; at least three distinct features of the sequence are discussed (can include editing choices, sound design, cinematography as well as narrative devices); the analysis explains how each feature contributes to the spectator's experience of the technique (e.g. how a withheld close-up of a face leaves the spectator unsure of motive); the connection between micro choice and macro narrative meaning is explicit; specialist vocabulary is varied and accurate throughout.
Secure: Named sequence and technique; three features present; at least two linked to spectator positioning; generally accurate specialist vocabulary.
Developing: One or two features identified; technique named but not fully applied to the sequence; effect on spectator implied; may drift beyond the named sequence.
Emerging: Describes what happens in the scene; no analysis of narrative technique; no micro-level features; no spectator positioning.

practice_questions.text: Explain how David Bordwell's idea of narration as the 'formal organisation of story information' applies to a film you have studied. Use a specific scene to illustrate your answer.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for accurately summarising Bordwell's idea (narration organises what information the spectator receives and when); 1 mark for naming the film and a specific scene; 1 mark for identifying one specific narrative decision in that scene (e.g. withheld information, a non-linear jump, an ellipsis); 1 mark for explaining what that decision does to the spectator's understanding or experience at that moment; 1 mark for specialist vocabulary (narration, fabula, syuzhet, plot, withholding, ellipsis).

knowledge_checks.q: Which term describes the order in which events are presented to the audience on screen?
In Todorov's narrative model, what follows 'disruption'?
The event early in a narrative that forces the protagonist into a new situation is called the _____ incident.
The narrative technique of compressing time by omitting intervening events is called _____.
Match each narrative concept to its correct description:
right: All events in chronological order, including those not shown on screen
A framework dividing narrative into set-up, confrontation and resolution
The principle that each narrative event is motivated by a preceding one

flashcard_questions.q: What is the difference between plot and story in film analysis?
flashcard_questions.a: Plot is the order events appear on screen; story is the full chronological sequence.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the Russian term for the plot — the arrangement of events on screen?
What is the Russian term for the underlying chronological story?
What is an inciting incident in three-act structure?
flashcard_questions.a: The event that disrupts the protagonist's ordinary world and sets the main conflict in motion.

flashcard_questions.q: In three-act structure, which act is typically the longest?
flashcard_questions.a: Act 2, the confrontation, usually around half the film's running time.

flashcard_questions.q: What is ellipsis as a narrative technique?
flashcard_questions.a: Compressing time by omitting events, jumping forward without showing the intervening period.

flashcard_questions.q: What are the three stages of Todorov's equilibrium model?
What does Bordwell mean by narration as the 'formal organisation of story information'?
flashcard_questions.a: The film decides what to reveal, withhold and delay to shape the spectator's experience.

flashcard_questions.q: In Propp's model, what role does the 'donor' character perform?
flashcard_questions.a: Provides the hero with a gift, ability or piece of knowledge needed for the quest.

flashcard_questions.q: What effect does a non-linear narrative opening (starting at the ending) create for the spectator?
flashcard_questions.a: Dramatic irony — the spectator watches every scene knowing how it ends.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the climax in narrative structure?
flashcard_questions.a: The point of highest tension or emotional intensity, typically near the end of Act 2 or start of Act 3.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is withholding information a significant narrative tool?
flashcard_questions.a: It controls what the spectator knows, creating suspense, mystery or a powerful later revelation.

glossary_terms.definition: The sequence of events as they are presented to the audience in the film, regardless of when they actually occurred in the story world.
All the events in a narrative taken in their real chronological order, including events referred to but not shown on screen.
A screenwriting framework that divides a narrative into three sections: set-up (Act 1), confrontation (Act 2), and resolution (Act 3).
The event early in a narrative that disrupts the protagonist's everyday world and sets the main conflict in motion.
The point of highest tension or emotional intensity in a narrative, typically near the end of Act 2 or beginning of Act 3.
The principle that each event in a narrative is motivated by a preceding event and produces a subsequent one, creating forward momentum.
A narrative technique in which time is compressed by omitting events, jumping forward without showing the intervening period.
In Todorov's narrative model, the state of balance or normality at the beginning of a story.
The roles characters play in a narrative according to Propp's model: hero, villain, donor, helper, dispatcher, princess and false hero.
The way a film organises and presents story information to the spectator, deciding what to reveal, withhold and delay.

items.title: Lessons from the Screenplay — The Matrix: Exposition in Action
items.description: Shows how The Matrix uses its three-act structure to control the spectator's knowledge — exactly the plot vs story analysis this lesson covers. (~8 min)

items.title: Lessons from the Screenplay — How A Christmas Carol Demonstrates Five-Act Structure
items.description: Clear walkthrough of narrative structure theory applied to a familiar story — brilliant for consolidating Todorov's equilibrium model. (~8 min)

items.title: Lessons from the Screenplay — The Hidden Structure of Before Sunset
items.description: Examines how films can embed complex structural choices in apparently simple conversations — great for understanding non-linear narration. (~10 min)

items.title: Hitchcock/Truffaut (2015)
items.description: Contemporary directors discuss the master of narrative suspense and how he structured spectator knowledge — Bordwell's narration theory in action.
